web_evidence.title: The Bonfire of the Vanities
web_evidence.note: The publisher-authorized prologue sustains third-person narration of the Mayor, moving between external action and his thoughts; visible first-person language is localized as thought or speech.

web_evidence.title: Wealth and Virtue: Utopian Republicanism in Tom Wolfe’s The Bonfire of the Vanities
web_evidence.note: The peer-reviewed analysis describes all 31 chapters and the epilogue as told by an extradiegetic, heterodiegetic narrator who moves among distinct character focalizers.

web_evidence.title: Tom Wolfe Writing Styles in The Bonfire of the Vanities
web_evidence.note: The explicit point-of-view discussion identifies a third-person omniscient narrator focalized primarily through Sherman McCoy, Kramer, and Peter Fallow.

search_log: Searched "The Bonfire of the Vanities Tom Wolfe excerpt first chapter publisher" and opened Macmillan's authorized prologue; Google Books supplied mainly catalog copy and a table of contents, so it was not used as person evidence.

Searched "The Bonfire of the Vanities point of view third person narrator scholarly" and "The Bonfire of the Vanities heterodiegetic narrator"; opened the journal PDF and the explicit BookRags point-of-view page.

Searched the title with "first-person", "alternating point of view", "narrator", and "free indirect discourse"; found no credible evidence of sustained first- or second-person base sections. Some results concerned the film's Peter Fallow voice-over or embedded character thoughts rather than the novel's base narrator.

Checked Google Books, the Paris Review author interview, and an unauthorized excerpt compilation as discovery material; they did not add stronger whole-book person evidence than the publisher excerpt and structural scholarship.
person_note: The diagnostic quotes repeatedly show a nonparticipating narrator describing Sherman, Kramer, the Mayor, and other characters while entering their thoughts through free-indirect discourse. First-person forms occur in direct speech or explicitly localized thought, and generic you passages are not sustained second-person narration. The authorized opening independently demonstrates this third-person technique, while peer-reviewed whole-book analysis identifies an extradiegetic, heterodiegetic narrator moving among focalizers; an explicit study guide corroborates third-person omniscience. The clipped and popularity-selected nature of several quotes is the main evidence limitation, but the whole-book structural source resolves it, and no credible alternating-person evidence was found.
